title: 100 Pieces of Gossip You May Not Know About Apple's New Chief Design Officer
excerpt: 100 small facts, no more and no fewer. It's a long read. Can you make it to the end?
body:
100 small facts, no more and no fewer. It's a long read. Can you make it to the end?

1. Sir Jonathan Paul Ive, Apple's senior designer, has just been promoted to chief design officer. He keeps his leadership of all Apple hardware and UI design and will take on [a wider range of projects](http://money.163.com/15/0526/08/AQHF4EHU00251LK6.html), likely including the design of two major ones: Apple's retail stores and its new campus.

2. Apple's top designer is dyslexic.

3. At Macworld in 2003, a *Wired* reporter left a backpack in the hall after talking to him. Ive carried it around all night, hoping to give it back.

4. Most of the iMacs, iPods, iPads and iPhones in people's hands were designed by him. He made *Time* magazine's 2013 list of the 100 most influential people, and the British Crown has made him a Knight Commander of the Order of the British Empire.

5. His birthplace, Chingford, is the home of the sirloin steak. His father was a silversmith and teacher, his mother a psychotherapist, and he has a younger sister.

6. As a child he took apart every manufactured object he could. The fun of taking things apart later grew into an interest in how things are made: how they work, what shape they take and what they are made of.

7. Ive's father, an educator, cared deeply about design and technology. Through his teaching he helped make design and technology part of the core curriculum in British schools. Like father, like son.

8. On walks, his father would point at a streetlight and ask: "Why do you think these lamps are different? How does the light spread downward? What kind of weather might affect which streetlight people choose?"

9. Just after Ive turned 12, the family moved to Stafford. Classmates at Walton High School remember him as a good kid: "dark-haired, a bit chubby, and modest."

10. The school had a computer lab, but perhaps because of his dyslexia, typing code one key at a time was hard work for the young Ive.

11. One Christmas present he received was unusual: free run of his father's workshop, with his father's help to make any craft piece he wanted.

12. Because of this upbringing, Ive told Walter Isaacson, Steve Jobs's biographer: "I've always understood the beauty of things made by hand. I came to see that what really matters is the care you put into a product. I despise products that show their makers were careless."

13. At 13, Ive knew he wanted to "draw and make things," though he had not settled on what to make. He began to think about designing everything, from cars to furniture to jewelry and boats.

14. His father named four activities, "drawing, sketching, talking and discussing," as the keys to the creative process. He argued that designers must dare to take risks and accept that they "cannot know everything." He believed young people needed to be taught perseverance, so there was never a moment to slacken. These ideas stayed with Ive throughout the development of the iMac and the iPhone.

15. As a teenager he drove himself to school every day. He liked to comb his long black hair into spikes several inches high, but the spikes got crushed against the car roof, so he had to open the sunroof.

16. Teachers remember that whenever Ive's orange Fiat pulled into the school, a wild tuft of black hair stuck up through the roof.

17. For university Ive chose Newcastle Polytechnic (now Northumbria University) in the north of England, which had the best industrial design program in Britain.

18. His tuition was paid in full by the Roberts Weaver Group. The firm saw his "undeniable talent" and sponsored him at 1,500 euros a year, hoping he would join it after graduating.

19. Ive missed the first two days of his first term because a design he made in high school had won an award and he had to go and collect it.

20. In first year Ive took a sculpture class. The professor was allergic to plaster dust, yet he respected every student's work: before discussing a piece, however poor, he would carefully brush the dust off it.

21. From that professor Ive learned to respect the work: "You have to respect the work. If you don't respect it yourself, how can you ask anyone else to?"

22. His first year at university was hard, and he buried himself in his work.

23. In his second year he began his first internship, two terms long, at the Roberts Weaver Group. The university required two internships of a year each.

24. There Ive met the senior designer Clive Grinyer, who would become a close friend despite the eight years between them.

25. At the time Ive wore an odd shoulder-length haircut, with the fringe combed back and standing straight up. Grinyer recalls that "he looked like a bottle brush."

26. The young man was extremely modest.

27. He was soon assigned to design a line of leather goods and wallets for Japan's Zebra Co., Ltd. **These wallets were the first white products Ive designed**, the start of his lifelong preference for the color.

28. Later he designed a pen in white plastic, with rubber studs along the side like little teeth that made it easy to grip.

![The TX2 pen Ive designed for Zebra](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160608130859ptL5EwNiqmTzJ8Ho.jpg-w600)

29. Ive noticed that people like to fiddle with a pen when they are not writing, so he added a "fidget device," a small ball and clip, to the top. Decoration that invites touch like this runs through all his work.

30. The pen, model TX2, went into production quickly, something unheard of for an intern, and it sold well in Japan for years.

31. When other students built a dozen models, Ive would build more than a hundred. They differed only in small details, but laid out in a row they looked like an evolution.

32. Ive became the first undergraduate to win the RSA travel bursary twice, and his graduation show earned him the highest grade of degree honours awarded in Britain.

33. In his second year he married his childhood sweetheart. That was also the year he first took notice of Apple.

34. But he kept his promise. After graduating he did not go to Apple but to the Roberts Weaver Group, which had paid for his studies, and looked elsewhere only after the firm ended his contract for its own reasons.

35. In September 1992, at 27, Ive took a full-time job at Apple and, with his wife's support, moved the family to San Francisco.

36. John Markoff of *The New York Times* described their home: a fireplace, extremely spare interiors, a small television sitting on an expensive record player, and wheels under almost every piece of furniture so it could be moved anywhere.

37. The lighting was futuristic: a red globe hung overhead like a planet. Yet there was not a personal computer in sight.

38. Ive's first tough assignment at Apple was the second-generation Newton handheld, and his design was outstanding. He soon won several of the industry's top awards, including a gold award for industrial design excellence.

39. Ive hates accepting awards in public.

40. Robert Brunner was the man who brought Ive to Apple. He asked to work with Ive at least three times; he was, in effect, the talent scout who discovered him.

41. When Ive was 29, Brunner decided to leave Apple. Brunner, whose later work includes the Kindle and Beats headphones, strongly recommended Ive as his successor. **He said Ive had "a holistic mind, like a craftsman: he likes to see the whole picture but is absorbed in every detail. I knew he had what it takes to succeed."**

42. Then Apple fell into a period of chaos, which troubled Ive.

43. Luckily, just as Ive was preparing to go back to Britain, Jobs returned to Apple in shorts and sneakers and told everyone: "We're going to make great products, not money."

44. It was that sentence that kept Ive at Apple.

![Jony Ive and Steve Jobs](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160608130900YrDyi5JC4cwuXZzF.jpg-w600)

45. Jobs never had formal design training, but he had a keen eye for design from childhood, and many of his ideas about design overlapped with Ive's.

46. Both had fathers who were a good influence. Jobs's father liked to do things perfectly. If he built a fence, the back had to be as good as the front. "He cared even about the parts you couldn't see."

47. Jobs planned to get the all-in-one Apple computer to market within a few months; otherwise Apple might have to close. Ive began searching for a design theme for this network computer, wanting a product that "makes people feel good."

48. The result, the iMac, looked like this: through its translucent shell you could see the silver electromagnetic shielding inside. It was a cross between a transparent thermos and a car taillight.

49. During the design, Ive had his designers bring every colored transparent object they could find into the studio for inspiration: old see-through thermoses, BMW taillights, cheap picnic tableware.

50. They studied a whole shelf of translucent objects, examining their quality, texture, depth and internal structure.

51. The color finally chosen was a blue inspired by a small piece of blue-green sea glass from a beach, its surface lightly frosted. It made people want to touch the machine and told them it was a friendly design.

52. Ive made mistakes too.

53. The round "puck" mouse he designed proved an ergonomic flop. It slid around the desk, always pointed the wrong way, and was too small for many adult hands.

54. Ive did not work alone. He was good at teamwork, and designers such as Daniele De Iuliis worked closely with him.

55. These industrial designers were obsessive. "If we were designing a switch, there might be more than 50 models of household switches and volume switches. We'd study the edges and ask how far it should stand out, whether it should have a pivot, whether it should be round, whether it should be metal or plastic, and so on."

![Apple's industrial design team at work](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160608130900oPJ28p0wgz67SV9E.jpg-w600)

56. With the new iBook, a crystal-clear, simple, small rectangular "ice" notebook, Ive's design language shifted from multicolored plastic to plain white and black polycarbonate, a look later carried by the iMac and iPod.

57. For more professional products, however, he would redesign in anodized aluminum.

58. By 2000, Ive had completed four major designs. He and his team then tried to bring their most ambitious product to market: the Power Mac Cube.

59. The Cube debuted in September 2000, and in the following months it sold poorly, at one-third of projections.

60. The machine flopped in the market but still had plenty of admirers inside the company, because it made major advances in manufacturing and miniaturization.

61. On February 9, 2001, Ive's industrial design studio moved from Valley Green Drive, across the road from Apple's headquarters, into a spacious area inside headquarters, where it remains today.

62. With the studio now at the heart of Apple, Jobs could work more closely with Ive's team. The move showed everyone that the design team's standing in the company had risen.

63. **In Ive's words: "The industrial design studio truly hears the heartbeat of the company."**

64. The designers got the best of everything. Headquarters had every piece of furniture custom-made to the studio's specifications for Ive and his designers: desks, chairs, even drinking glasses.

65. Ive's office is a glass cube 12 feet high and 12 feet wide, the only private office in the studio. Its front wall and door are glass with stainless steel fittings, just like an Apple store.

66. Apart from a few shelves, the walls are bare and white, with no family photos or award certificates. The furniture is a desk, a chair and a lamp.

67. Ive's leather chair is a Supporto from the British office-furniture maker Hille. He considers the chair, made of leather and aluminum, a design masterpiece.

68. The designers work in a huge open-plan space, and it is a mess: boxes, parts, prototypes, even bicycles and toys lie everywhere.

69. **Ive is a diehard fan of electronic music.**

70. Most Apple employees, including some executives, are not allowed into the design studio. It is probably the most secretive department at Apple.

71. Apple takes secrecy to the extreme, so the designers have almost no contact with the media and little public profile. They have won every major award and everyone in the industry knows them, yet to the general public they remain unknown.

72. Because they are routinely kept out of sight of the media and headhunters, the team calls itself "the design team behind the Iron Curtain."

73. Ive's industrial design team has become a close-knit family, and many of its members have worked together for decades.

74. Ive is a veteran sketcher. But colleagues say **his sketches are really rough**: "The lines are shaky, and the way he draws is really interesting."

75. Ive's role at Apple kept changing. He moved gradually from designer to manager, responsible not only for running the team but also for hiring.

76. For all his effectiveness as a leader, Ive remains a soft-spoken English gentleman.

77. Compared with heads of other Apple departments, Ive is very protective of his team: "He will take the blame for the whole team himself."

78. Ive's team is tight-knit, but its relations with other departments are less cordial. An Apple engineer who worked with the industrial design team for nearly 10 years said: "Working with Jony and his team made me feel constrained. It always reminded me how prominent the design team is at Apple."

79. The designers believe social life and work cannot be separated.

80. They often hire a limousine, load it with Bollinger champagne, and head out together to eat and drink.

81. Many designers like to bring their children to the studio, but Ive has always kept the bustle of Apple away from his wife and their twin sons. He does not want the boys to follow him into design.

82. **Making the iPod white was Ive's idea.**

83. He saw white as the opposite of colorful: "It's not just a color but a neutral attitude, at once obvious and neutral between two extremes."

84. The iPod earned him the nickname "Jony iPod" and opened an era of white tech products.

85. Ive drives fast and loves supercars.

86. The Mac mini went into production at Foxconn, with the iPod mini and other products soon after.

87. After the SARS outbreak in 2003, Ive and some team members were forced into quarantine at Foxconn, which delayed the project.

88. Over the years the rising status of Ive's industrial design team has shown in many ways. On business trips in China, ordinary design staff took taxis, while the industrial designers were picked up in stretch limousines, and they stayed in better-rated hotels. Ten years earlier, everyone had been treated the same.

89. Before the first iPhone went on sale, the oversized gap between the glass screen and the stainless steel bezel kept catching the designers' beards.

90. While designing the iPad, Ive made 20 prototypes of different sizes and screen aspect ratios and lined them up on a display stand in the studio for himself and Jobs to play with.

91. They did this for almost every product, then picked the one they liked best.

92. Ive goes back to London three or four times a year and travels the world now and then.

93. As Northumbria University's most famous graduate, Ive is seen by fellow alumni as a priceless asset.

94. He often returns to give talks, yet the university refuses to discuss him or reveal anything about his time there, simply to protect the relationship.

95. Jobs thought very highly of Ive.

![Jony Ive](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160608130901SNO1uWb6Kp3zyQn7.jpg-w600)

96. After Jobs died, Ive opened his eulogy with an aside: **"Steve used to say to me — and he used to say this a lot — 'Hey Jony, here's a dopey idea.' And sometimes they were. Really dopey. Sometimes they were truly dreadful. But sometimes they took the air from the room, and they left us both completely silent."**

97. The eulogy was by turns funny, moving and thought-provoking, and it ended with "Steve, thank you."

98. The day before Jobs died, Tim Cook unveiled the iPhone 4S at the Yerba Buena Center in San Francisco. Jobs's seat was marked "Reserved." Notably, Ive was absent too.

99. Jobs's death notwithstanding, 2012 turned out to be a lucky year for Ive and for Apple.

100. That year Ive's name appeared on the Queen's New Year Honours list. For services to design he was made a Knight Commander of the Order of the British Empire, the second time he had been honored this way.

Note: About 90% of this article is drawn from *Jony Ive: The Genius Behind Apple's Greatest Products* by Leander Kahney (Chinese edition translated by Wang Qi, Yue Hui and Wang Wenya).
